newsitem.title: KENYA: Police battle rioting students in Nairobi.
newsitem.headline: Police battle rioting students in Nairobi.

text.p: Thousands of students took to the heart of Nairobi on Monday, stoning cars and clashing with riot police a week after the worst political unrest in Kenya in seven years.

Reuters reporters at the scene said thousands of Kenya Polytechnic students seized control of Haile Selassie Avenue, a major road through the city centre, throwing stones and demanding constitutional reforms before a general election.
They said dozens of riot and crack General Service Unit (GSU) police arrived in minutes and fired teargas and rubber bullets in a bid to drive students back into the polytechnic campus.
But groups of students repeatedly ran out into the avenue, threw stones and ran back on to the campus. Some police picked up stones and threw them back when they ran out of teargas.

The students blocked almost the entire length of the broad Haile Selassie Avenue with burning tyres and makeshift barricades. GSU units moved in to secure the Central Bank building and riot police protected the nearby U.S. embassy.
Some students shouted slogans against the Asian community, accusing people of Asian origin of getting rich at their expense. Student activists distributed rocks from baskets to colleagues.
After reinforcements arrived, hundreds of riot police cleared students off the avenue and stormed the polytechnic as other officers fired bullets over the heads of students.

Witnesses said a Reuters photographer was hit on the head by a police baton in the riots on Monday, one week after nine people were killed during unrest in Nairobi and other towns and cities and fierce clashes between demonstrators and riot police.

Opposition-backed groups demand constitutional reforms before presidential and parliamentary elections this year. No date has been set for the polls but President Daniel arap Moi has said there is too little time for them before the election.
Authorities ordered Nairobi University and Jomo Kenyatta University closed indefinitely last week and their students were sent home following several days of clashes with riot police and unrest.
In addition to the constitutional reform issue, the country's students have been angered by a draft parliamentary bill requiring the expulsion of students who fail to pay their fees.
Anglican Archbishop David Gitari on Sunday verbally attacked Moi from the pulpit at Nairobi's All Saints Cathedral at a ceremonial "cleansing" and re-dedication after last week's riots.
Police threw teargas into the cathedral and beat opposition and reform leaders when people fleeing a confrontation between demonstrators and police sought refuge there last Monday.
"Blood cannot be shed in a holy place in vain. The government must now put into motion constitutional reforms," the archbishop said. "There is still hope that the cries of the people will be heard."
Moslem preacher and one of Moi's most outspoken critics, Sheikh Khalid Balala, was at the service after being allowed by authorities to return on Saturday from two years' exile in Germany.

Moi, 73 and in power for the last 19 years, said last Friday he would take action against any attempt to bring chaos to the country and challenged the opposition to take the debate on reforms to parliament, where his ruling party has a majority.
